correctness.rationale: The atomic two-types of the transitive, inverse-traversable labelled Cayley structure depend only on signed-generator element equalities and presence of a generic difference; explicit two-variable formulas distinguish each profile. Balanced composition of signed word paths uses exactly three names, recovering the marked free-group kernel. Short spanning-tree edge-relators force a marked quotient of the smaller group onto the larger one, yielding the logarithmic rank bound. The three-pebble cycle gap invariant shows logarithmic lower order. The standalone finite checker returns VERIFY_OK, but unrestricted claims rest on the proof.

originality.rationale: This sharp complete adjacent-variable classification with a diameter-sensitive distinguishing-depth bound does not follow from the inspected statements on full first-order decidability for Cayley graphs or general pebble games. Searches of related terms and published mathematical findings found no directly equivalent or broader coverage. However both the 2002 Kuske–Lohrey report and 2005 journal article lacked accessible full-text comparison, so historical priority remains provisional.
residual_risks: The full 2002 technical report mentioned in the STACS paper and the full 2005 expanded paper were not available; existing explicit bounded-width proofs in them would diminish or eliminate novelty.
Search-based absence is not uniqueness proof; unrelated published versions of short distinguishing-relator bounds may exist.
The one-generator cyclic special case is a lower-bound illustration, not asserted as a wholly new standalone result.

value.rationale: Complete adjacent-width theory for all marked finite groups is a natural expressive-power boundary: FO2 forgets all but a finite signed-generator equality profile, whereas FO3 reconstructs every group relator, including distinctions among equally sized nonabelian/abelian groups. The diameter-sensitive logarithmic depth bound and matching logarithmic-order cycle obstruction quantify that transition without an arbitrary finite cutoff. This is substantially more than a narrow computed special case.
